what_it_does: In cloud data centers, some CPU cores sit idle while their assigned virtual machine (VM) waits for network requests or user input. A common trick called 'core harvesting' lets the system temporarily lend those idle cores to batch-processing VMs to squeeze out more useful work. However, doing this purely in software is too slow: handing a core to a new VM requires notifying the operating system supervisor (the hypervisor), flushing the core's address-translation cache (TLB — a small table that speeds up memory look-ups), and clearing the data cache, all of which takes too long for workloads that must respond in microseconds. HardHarvest moves the entire lending mechanism into hardware. A new hardware scheduler watches for idle cores and assigns them to batch tasks directly, without waking the hypervisor. Smart cache-replacement rules carve out a protected slice of the cache for the primary VM's data, so shifting to the borrowing VM does not evict important data. The hardware also monitors the primary VM's request queue and yanks the borrowed core back the instant the primary VM needs it, before any slowdown is felt.
